Column1: An enterprise is deploying internet-facing applications on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) and wants automatic, always-on protection against large-scale volumetric and protocol-based attacks that could disrupt service availability. Which OCI security service is purpose-built to mitigate these Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks at the infrastructure edge?
Column4:
❌ OCI Web Application Firewall (WAF) — Incorrect
• Protects against application-layer attacks (OWASP Top 10, SQL injection, XSS)
• Does not provide full infrastructure-level DDoS mitigation
• Exam trap: WAF is often mistaken as DDoS protection, but it operates at Layer 7
• Incorrect
Column6:
❌ OCI Cloud Guard — Incorrect
• Detects misconfigurations and risky activities using security recipes
• Provides visibility and recommendations, not real-time traffic mitigation
• Exam trap: Monitoring ≠ protection
• Incorrect
Column8:
❌ OCI Identity and Access Management (IAM) — Incorrect
• Manages users, groups, policies, and authentication
• Has no role in traffic filtering or attack mitigation
• Exam trap: IAM secures access, not availability
• Incorrect
Column10:
✔ OCI DDoS Protection — Correct
• Native, always-on service designed specifically to mitigate DDoS attacks
• Protects OCI edge infrastructure automatically at no additional cost
• Mitigates volumetric, protocol, and resource exhaustion attacks
• Follows Oracle’s shared responsibility security model
• Reference: Official Oracle OCI DDoS Protection documentation
• Correct
Column12:
❌ OCI Security Zones — Incorrect
• Enforces security best practices via policy-based compartments
• Prevents risky configurations but does not handle live attack traffic
• Exam trap: Preventive governance ≠ attack mitigation
• Incorrect
Column16: For the OCI Foundations Associate (1Z0-1085-25) exam, remember: OCI DDoS Protection is the only service explicitly designed to defend against Distributed Denial of Service attacks. Other security services may monitor, restrict access, or protect applications—but DDoS mitigation is handled exclusively by OCI DDoS Protection.
Column17: Security Services

Column1: An enterprise operates several Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) tenancies for different business units. The security team wants to centrally manage user authentication and access policies using an external corporate identity provider, ensuring consistent governance and simplified compliance across all tenancies. Which OCI IAM capability enables this approach?
Column4:
❌ Dynamic Groups — Incorrect
• Used to grant permissions to OCI resources (like compute instances)
• Does not manage user identities across multiple OCI tenancies
• Exam trap: Confusing workload identity management with user identity federation
Column6:
❌ Compartments — Incorrect
• Logical isolation of resources within a single tenancy
• Cannot centralize identity or access across multiple OCI accounts
• Exam trap: Assuming compartments span multiple tenancies
Column8:
✔ Federation — Correct
• Integrates OCI IAM with an external Identity Provider (IdP) such as Azure AD, Okta, or Oracle Identity Cloud Service
• Enables centralized authentication and access governance across multiple OCI tenancies
• Simplifies compliance, user lifecycle management, and enterprise-scale access control
• Reference: Oracle IAM Federation supports cross-tenancy identity management using trusted IdPs
• Correct
Column10:
❌ Resource Manager — Incorrect
• Infrastructure-as-Code service for provisioning OCI resources
• Has no role in identity federation or access governance
• Exam trap: Confusing governance automation with identity management
Column12:
❌ Defined Tags — Incorrect
• Used for resource classification, cost tracking, and governance
• Does not control authentication or access permissions
• Exam trap: Mixing tagging-based governance with IAM access control
Column16: For centralized user authentication and access management across multiple OCI tenancies, OCI relies on IAM Federation. Compartments and tags are governance tools within a tenancy, while federation integrates OCI with external identity providers to streamline enterprise-wide access control.
Column17: Security Services (OCI IAM)

Column1: An organization wants to proactively improve its overall security posture in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The security team requires a service that continuously evaluates resource configurations, detects misconfigurations and risky activities, and provides actionable recommendations to remediate security issues across compartments. Which OCI service best fulfills this requirement?
Column4:
❌ OCI Security Zones — Incorrect
• Enforces predefined security policies and prevents non-compliant actions
• Does not continuously monitor or recommend fixes
• Exam trap: Often confused with Cloud Guard because both relate to security posture
• Incorrect
Column6:
✔ OCI Cloud Guard — Correct
• Continuously monitors OCI resources for:
  o Misconfigurations
  o Risky activities
  o Security weaknesses
• Detects problems using detectors
• Provides actionable remediation guidance using responders
• Integrates with OCI services and compartments
• Aligned with official OCI security posture management behavior
• Correct
Column8:
❌ OCI Audit — Incorrect
• Records API calls and user activities for compliance and investigation
• Does not analyze risk posture or provide remediation recommendations
• Exam trap: Logging ≠ security posture management
• Incorrect
Column10:
❌ OCI Identity and Access Management (IAM) — Incorrect
• Manages users, groups, policies, and authentication
• Does not monitor resources or detect misconfigurations
• Exam trap: IAM controls access, not posture
• Incorrect
Column12:
❌ OCI Logging Analytics — Incorrect
• Provides log aggregation, analysis, and insights
• Requires logs as input and does not directly assess security posture
• Incorrect
Column16: OCI Cloud Guard is Oracle’s native security posture management service. It continuously monitors resources, detects risks, and recommends remediation actions. For any exam question mentioning continuous monitoring, security posture, detectors, or recommended fixes, Cloud Guard is the correct answer.
Column17: Security Services

Column1: In Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), which of the following statements correctly describe features or capabilities associated with a Virtual Cloud Network (VCN)? Select two.
Column3: Network Security Groups (NSGs) allow you to define virtual firewall rules that control traffic for groups of resources within a VCN.
Column4: ✔ Network Security Groups (NSGs) — Correct\n• Allows creation of logical firewall rules for VCN resources without using subnet-level security lists.\n• Reference: OCI VCN Documentation
Column5: FastConnect provides high-bandwidth, low-latency private connections directly between OCI VCNs and external data centers.
Column6: ❌ FastConnect — Incorrect\n• Provides private connectivity between on-premises data centers and OCI, but it is not a native VCN component.\n• Exam trap: Confusing private connectivity with internal VCN capabilities.
Column7: File Storage Service automatically configures VCN routing rules to provide secure file sharing between compute instances.
Column8: ❌ File Storage Service — Incorrect\n• A storage service, does not configure VCN routing rules automatically.\n• Exam trap: Misleading because storage resources are accessible via VCN, but not a VCN component.
Column9: NAT Gateway enables outbound internet access for resources in a private subnet without exposing them to inbound traffic.
Column10: ✔ NAT Gateway — Correct\n• Enables outbound-only internet access for private subnets, preserving security by blocking inbound traffic.\n• Reference: OCI NAT Gateway Documentation
Column11: Object Storage Buckets can be attached to a VCN to allow direct network-level access to storage resources.
Column12: ❌ Object Storage Buckets — Incorrect\n• Cannot be attached to a VCN; access is via public endpoints or private endpoints, not a VCN feature.\n• Exam trap: Confusing OCI storage services with VCN networking features.
Column16: VCN components = networking-focused features: NSG, IGW, NAT Gateway, DRG, route tables, subnets. Storage services (Block, File, Object) are not VCN components. Exam trap: Mixing storage integration with networking services.
Column17: Core OCI Services → Networking → Virtual Cloud Network (VCN) components

Column1: An e-commerce company plans to host a critical customer-facing application on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) that must remain operational even if an entire data center experiences an outage. Which deployment strategy provides the highest availability and fault tolerance according to OCI best practices?
Column3: Deploy the application in a single Availability Domain, using multiple Fault Domains within that AD.
Column4:
❌ Deploy the application in a single Availability Domain, using multiple Fault Domains within that AD — Incorrect
• Only protects against hardware-level failures in that AD.
• Does not protect against an entire AD outage.
• Exam trap: Candidates may confuse FD-level isolation with AD-level resilience.
Column5: Deploy the application across multiple Availability Domains within a single OCI Region.
Column6:
❌ Deploy the application across multiple Availability Domains within a single OCI Region — Incorrect
• Protects against an AD-level failure within that Region.
• Does not provide geographic redundancy in case the entire Region fails.
• Partial solution, but not the highest availability possible.
Column7: Deploy the application across multiple Regions, but restrict resources to a single Availability Domain per Region.
Column8: ❌ Deploy the application across multiple Regions, but restrict resources to a single Availability Domain per Region — Incorrect\n• Provides geographic redundancy but leaves each Region vulnerable to an AD-level failure.\n• Misconception: Multi-Region alone does not guarantee maximum fault tolerance.
Column9: Deploy the application across multiple Availability Domains in multiple OCI Regions.
Column10:
✔ Deploy the application across multiple Availability Domains in multiple OCI Regions — Correct
• Correct approach for maximum availability and resiliency.
• Protects against:
  o AD-level failures (via multiple ADs in each Region)
  o Regional failures (via multiple Regions)
• Follows OCI recommended best practices for critical, highly available applications.
• Reference: Oracle Docs – Regions, Availability Domains, and Fault Domains
Column16: Always deploy critical applications across multiple ADs for local resiliency. For maximum fault tolerance, also deploy across multiple Regions. Single AD or single Region deployments are not sufficient for mission-critical workloads.

Column1: When designing a cloud-native application on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), you need compute resources that can automatically scale to handle variable workloads while minimizing infrastructure management. Which two OCI Compute services are best suited for this requirement?
Column4: ✔ OCI Functions — Correct • Serverless compute platform; automatically scales, no server management required. • Reference: OCI Functions Documentation
Column6: ❌ OCI Virtual Machine (VM) Instances — Incorrect • You must manage the OS and patching; scaling requires manual configuration (e.g., Autoscaling), so it’s not fully serverless. • Exam trap: Candidates often confuse “VM scaling” with serverless.
Column8: ✔ OCI Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) — Correct • Managed Kubernetes service; control plane fully managed, nodes can autoscale using Node Pools. • Minimizes server management while supporting scalable workloads. • Reference: OKE Documentation
Column10: ❌ OCI Bare Metal Instances — Incorrect • Full control over hardware and OS; requires manual scaling. • Classic trap: thinking “more capacity” means “serverless” — it does not.
Column12: ❌ OCI Dedicated Compute Hosts — Incorrect • Dedicated physical host for your instances; requires full management. • Not suitable for serverless or minimal infrastructure management.
Column16: Serverless / fully managed compute services → OCI Functions, OKE with autoscaling. Managed VM/Bare Metal/Dedicated Hosts → You control infrastructure → not serverless. Exam trap: Don’t confuse “VM Instances with autoscaling” as fully serverless — autoscaling doesn’t remove OS/hardware management responsibility.

Column1: Which of the following statements correctly describe the function of a security list in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI)?
Column3: A security list defines rules to allow or deny traffic at the subnet level by specifying ingress and egress rules.
Column4: ✔ A security list defines rules to allow or deny traffic at the subnet level by specifying ingress and egress rules. • Security lists are applied at the subnet level. • They define stateful ingress and egress rules that determine which traffic is allowed. • Reference: OCI Security Lists Documentation
Column5: A security list manages IAM policies and controls which users can access specific resources.

Column10: ❌ A security list is preconfigured to deny all incoming and outgoing traffic by default. • Security lists are empty by default; they do not block traffic automatically. Rules must be defined by the user.
Column16: Security lists control network traffic at the subnet level via ingress/egress rules. They do not manage users, encrypt data, or block all traffic by default. Exam trap: confusing security lists with IAM policies or encryption mechanisms.

Column1: In Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), the Shared Security Model defines how security responsibilities are divided. Which of the following accurately describes the OCI Shared Security Model?

Column4: ✔ Oracle secures the physical infrastructure and network, while customers manage security for their applications, data, and operating system. • Correct — reflects OCI standard Shared Security Model. • Oracle secures the cloud infrastructure; customers secure their guest OS, applications, and data. • Reference: Oracle OCI Security Overview
Column5: Customers are responsible for the entire security stack, including hardware, hypervisor, and network.
Column6: ❌ Customers are responsible for the entire security stack, including hardware, hypervisor, and network. • Incorrect — customers do not manage physical infrastructure, hypervisor, or network. • Classic exam trap: Overestimating customer responsibility in IaaS.
Column7: Oracle is responsible for all security aspects, including customer applications and data.

Column9: Security responsibilities are outsourced entirely to third-party vendors, with no obligations for Oracle or customers.
Column10: ❌ Security responsibilities are outsourced entirely to third-party vendors, with no obligations for Oracle or customers. • Incorrect — Oracle and customers both share responsibilities; third-party vendors are optional, not default. • Exam trap: distractor using extreme statements.

Column1: An enterprise is migrating a multi-tiered e-commerce application to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The application architecture includes: • Web Frontend: Highly unpredictable traffic with seasonal spikes. • Application Layer: Moderate, predictable load with occasional batch jobs. • Database Layer: Critical, stable workload requiring high availability. • Dev/Test Environment: Non-production, intermittent usage for QA. The company aims to minimize costs without impacting performance or availability. Considering OCI compute pricing models, which approach best aligns with cost optimization and workload characteristics?
Column3: Deploy On-Demand Instances for the Web Frontend, Reserved Instances for the Application Layer, Reserved Instances for the Database Layer, and Always Free Resources for Dev/Test.
Column4: ✔ Web Frontend → On-Demand / Spot: Supports unpredictable traffic, flexible pricing, Spot acceptable if workload is fault-tolerant. • Application Layer → Reserved / On-Demand: Predictable moderate load favors Reserved for cost savings; On-Demand works if batch jobs are intermittent. • Database Layer → Reserved: Stable, mission-critical workload benefits from Reserved pricing. • Dev/Test → Always Free: Intermittent usage; free tier reduces costs. • Reference: OCI Compute Pricing Overview
Column5: Use Spot Instances for the Web Frontend, On-Demand Instances for the Application Layer, Reserved Instances for the Database Layer, and On-Demand Instances for Dev/Test
Column6: ❌ Spot is okay for fault-tolerant workloads, but Web Frontend requires minimal interruption; Dev/Test can use Always Free to reduce cost. • Classic exam trap: assuming all On-Demand is needed for Dev/Test.
Column7: Deploy On-Demand Instances for the Web Frontend, On-Demand Instances for the Application Layer, Reserved Instances for the Database Layer, and Always Free Resources for Dev/Test
Column8: ✔ Same as above — supports unpredictable frontend, predictable application, critical DB, and free Dev/Test
Column9: Deploy Reserved Instances for all layers including Dev/Test to maximize long-term savings
Column10: ❌ Reserved is cost-efficient for predictable workloads, not for highly variable Web Frontend or intermittent Dev/Test. Over-provisioning leads to unnecessary cost.
Column11: Use Spot Instances for the Web Frontend, Reserved Instances for Application Layer, Reserved Instances for Database Layer, and Always Free Resources for Dev/Test.
Column12:
•	Web Frontend → On-Demand / Spot: Supports unpredictable traffic, flexible pricing, Spot acceptable if workload is fault-tolerant.
•	Application Layer → Reserved / On-Demand: Predictable moderate load favors Reserved for cost savings; On-Demand works if batch jobs are intermittent.
•	Database Layer → Reserved: Stable, mission-critical workload benefits from Reserved pricing.
•	Dev/Test → Always Free: Intermittent usage; free tier reduces costs.
•	Reference: OCI Compute Pricing Overview
Column16: Match compute pricing models to workload types: Unpredictable → On-Demand or Spot; Predictable → Reserved; Critical DB → Reserved; Dev/Test → Always Free. Avoid assuming Reserved is always cheapest for all layers.
Column17: Getting Started with OCI, Core OCI Services, Governance and Administration, Cost Management

Column1: Under the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Shared Security Model, which two responsibilities are primarily managed by the customer to maintain security and compliance best practices?

Column13: Hardware Lifecycle Management of OCI Compute Hosts
Column14: ❌ Oracle owns and maintains all underlying hardware. Customers cannot modify or manage compute hardware.
Column16: OCI Shared Security Model: Oracle secures infrastructure and physical assets, while customers secure data, identities, applications, and network traffic. Always differentiate between physical/hardware responsibilities (Oracle) and logical/application/network responsibilities (Customer).

Column9: Users are billed hourly based on the number of users actively logging in.
Column10: Incorrect: OCI does not bill governance services based on user activity. Common trap: thinking “user activity = billing” like some SaaS offerings.
Column16: Governance and administration services like IAM, Policies, Compartments, and Audit are always free in OCI. Remember: resource usage (compute, storage, networking) is billed, but core governance features are not. Oracle exam often tries to confuse pay-per-use vs free foundational services.
Column17: Getting Started with OCI, Core OCI Services, Security Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: Which Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) service allows developers to provision fully managed MySQL instances, automates routine maintenance like backups and patching, and provides built-in high availability with replication for production workloads?
Column4: Primarily designed for Oracle Database workloads (Autonomous Transaction Processing or Autonomous Data Warehouse). Does not natively support MySQL. Exam trap: Many assume “Autonomous = any database type”
Column6: Fully managed MySQL database service in OCI. Provides automated backups, patching, updates. Built-in high availability through replication. Reference: Oracle Cloud MySQL Database Service Documentation
Column8: Designed for key-value and document store workloads, not relational databases. Exam trap: Confusing “NoSQL” for general database management
Column10: Object storage is for storing unstructured data (blobs, files). Not a database service; cannot run queries or manage MySQL workloads
Column12: Security and compliance service for databases, not a database itself
Column16: OCI MySQL Database Service = fully managed MySQL with automated maintenance and HA. Do not confuse with Autonomous Database (Oracle DB workloads) or NoSQL services. Exam often tests automation + HA + database type
Column17: Core OCI Services – Database Services

Column1: A global enterprise is designing a hybrid architecture to replicate mission-critical workloads between its on-premises data center and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) for business continuity and disaster recovery. The solution must provide private, dedicated connectivity, predictable low latency, and enhanced security without relying on the public internet. Which OCI networking service best satisfies these requirements?
Column4: Enables private access to Oracle services (Object Storage, Autonomous DB). Does not provide connectivity to on-premises environments. Exam Trap: Confusing Oracle service access with hybrid connectivity
Column6: Acts as a virtual router for connectivity. Requires FastConnect or VPN to establish actual on-prem connectivity. Exam Trap: DRG alone does not provide physical or dedicated links
Column8: Provides dedicated, private connectivity between on-premises and OCI. Offers low latency, high bandwidth, and predictable performance. Avoids public internet exposure, improving security. Officially recommended for hybrid DR and data replication scenarios. Reference: Oracle Help Center – OCI FastConnect Overview. Correct
Column10: Enables public internet access for VCN resources. Does not guarantee low latency or private connectivity. Exam Trap: Internet access ≠ enterprise-grade DR connectivity
Column12: Used to connect two OCI VCNs in different regions. Not applicable for on-premises to OCI connectivity. Exam Trap: Mixing VCN-to-VCN peering with hybrid architecture
Column16: For hybrid disaster recovery, OCI FastConnect is the preferred and exam-expected solution when requirements include private connectivity, minimal latency, and secure data synchronization between on-premises environments and OCI. VPN and internet-based options do not meet enterprise DR performance standards.
Column17: Core OCI Services, Networking, Hybrid Cloud Architecture

Column1: An enterprise security architect is reviewing Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) native services that help protect, monitor, and control access to cloud resources. Which three OCI services are specifically categorized as Security services that improve an organization’s security posture in OCI?
Column4: Manages users, groups, policies, and authentication. Core OCI Security service for access control. Enforces least-privilege access. Official OCI Security service. Correct
Column6: Continuously monitors OCI resources for security misconfigurations and risks. Provides detectors and responders. Central service for security posture management. Explicitly listed under OCI Security Services. Correct
Column8: Protects applications from common web attacks (SQL injection, XSS, etc.). Layer 7 security service integrated with OCI Load Balancer and Edge services. Recognized OCI Security service. Correct
Column10: Provides dedicated private connectivity between on-premises and OCI. Networking service, not a security service. Exam trap: Secure connectivity ≠ security service. Incorrect
Column12: Shared file system service for compute instances. Does not provide security monitoring or enforcement. Exam trap: Storage services may support encryption, but they are not classified as Security services. Incorrect
Column14: Infrastructure-as-Code service using Terraform. Focuses on provisioning, not security controls. Exam trap: Governance tools are not always security tools. Incorrect
Column16: OCI Security services are those that control access, detect threats, and protect workloads. For the 1Z0-1085-25 exam, remember that IAM, Cloud Guard, and WAF are explicitly classified as OCI Security services, while networking, storage, and provisioning services—even if “secure”—are not.
Column17: Security Services

Column1: In Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), which service is primarily responsible for organizing resources into compartments and controlling access through policies across a tenancy?
Column4: Used for storing unstructured data such as backups and media. Does not manage resource organization or user permissions. Exam trap: Confusing data storage services with governance services. Incorrect
Column6: Central governance service in OCI. Used to: Create and manage users, groups, and dynamic groups. Define compartments to logically organize resources. Write policies to control access to OCI resources. IAM operates at the tenancy level, making it essential for resource management. Fully aligned with Oracle Help Portal documentation. Correct
Column8: Provides virtual machines and bare metal instances. Does not handle access control or resource organization. Exam trap: Assuming core services manage governance. Incorrect
Column10: Used for networking and connectivity. Cannot manage identities, policies, or compartments. Exam trap: Confusing infrastructure components with management services. Incorrect
Column12: Provides persistent storage for compute instances. No role in organizing or securing OCI resources. Incorrect
Column16: For the OCI Foundations Associate (1Z0-1085-25) exam, always remember: Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the core service used to organize resources using compartments and control access using policies. No other OCI service provides this governance functionality.
Column17: Governance and Administration

Column1: An organization is planning a multi-region Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) deployment to support disaster recovery and is evaluating networking and storage-related costs. The architect wants to understand how OCI pricing affects data movement and replication across regions. Which statement correctly reflects OCI’s pricing model for such a multi-region architecture?
Column3: Data transfer between OCI services within the same region is free, while data transfer between different OCI regions is charged.
Column4: OCI allows free data transfer between services in the same region. Inter-region data transfer is charged, regardless of service type. This directly impacts multi-region HA and DR designs. Official behavior per Oracle Help Portal networking pricing documentation.
Column5: All ingress and egress network traffic to and from OCI regions is free of charge.
Column6: OCI does not charge for ingress traffic. Egress traffic to the internet is charged beyond the monthly free allowance. Exam trap: Assuming “free ingress” also means “free egress.”
Column7: Cross-region Block Volume replication does not incur any additional storage or network costs.
Column8: Block Volume replication across regions incurs additional charges for the target block volume storage and inter-region data transfer. Exam trap: Confusing availability-domain replication with cross-region replication.
Column9: Load Balancer traffic is always free, regardless of whether it is within the same region or across regions.
Column10: Load Balancer traffic is metered. Inter-region traffic flowing through Load Balancers is not free. Exam trap: Assuming managed services eliminate network transfer costs.
Column11: Object Storage replication across regions is included at no additional cost by default.
Column12: Cross-region Object Storage replication incurs storage costs in the destination region and inter-region data transfer charges. Exam trap: Assuming replication is “free” because it is automated.
Column16: For OCI multi-region architectures, ingress is free, same-region service-to-service traffic is free, but inter-region data transfer and replication always incur charges.
Column17: Getting Started with OCI, Core OCI Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: A financial services organization is migrating regulated workloads to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The security team requires that all sensitive data stored on OCI be encrypted at rest, and mandates that encryption keys must be owned, managed, and rotated by the customer rather than Oracle. Which OCI service or feature best satisfies this requirement?
Column4: Provides Key Management Service (KMS) and HSM-backed keys. Customers can create, store, rotate, disable, and delete encryption keys. Supports envelope encryption for OCI services and aligns with compliance requirements for customer-controlled encryption.
Column5: OCI Key Management integrated through IAM policies
Column6: IAM policies control access and authorization, not encryption key ownership. IAM does not create, store, rotate, or manage encryption keys. Exam trap: confusing access control with key management.
Column7: OCI Cloud Guard with encryption responder recipes
Column8: Cloud Guard is a security posture management and threat detection service. It can detect misconfigurations but does not manage encryption keys. Exam trap: assuming Cloud Guard enforces encryption automatically.
Column9: OCI Data Safe with automated encryption enforcement
Column10: Data Safe focuses on database security, auditing, and masking. It does not provide encryption key ownership or lifecycle management. Exam trap: mixing database security tooling with encryption key control.
Column11: OCI Object Storage default Oracle-managed encryption
Column12: Object Storage encrypts data at rest by default, but keys are Oracle-managed and do not give customers full control over encryption keys. Exam trap: default encryption ≠ customer-managed encryption.
Column16: When encryption at rest with full customer control over keys is required, OCI Vault with customer-managed keys is the correct solution.
Column17: Security Services

Column1: A financial services company is designing a disaster recovery (DR) architecture for an application hosted on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The requirement is to ensure automatic data redundancy and availability across different OCI regions to protect against a regional outage, with minimal operational overhead. Which OCI service and configuration best satisfy this requirement?
Column3: OCI Object Storage configured with Cross-Region Replication
Column4: Automatically replicates objects asynchronously to another OCI region, ensuring geographic redundancy and disaster recovery readiness with minimal operational overhead. Aligns with Oracle-recommended DR patterns.
Column5: OCI Autonomous Database with backups stored only in the same region
Column6: Backups stored in the same region do not protect against regional failures and do not provide geographic redundancy. Exam trap: Backups ≠ cross-region disaster recovery.
Column7: OCI Block Volume with manual snapshots retained locally
Column8: Local snapshots remain within the same region, require manual management, and do not meet geographic redundancy needs. Exam trap: Snapshots improve recovery, not regional resilience.
Column9: OCI Streaming Service with multiple partitions
Column10: Designed for real-time data ingestion, not disaster recovery or long-term geographic redundancy. Does not replicate data automatically across regions.
Column11: OCI Functions deployed in multiple availability domains
Column12: Availability Domains are within the same region and do not address multi-region disaster recovery. Exam trap: AD-level high availability ≠ regional DR.
Column16: For multi-region disaster recovery in OCI, Object Storage with Cross-Region Replication provides automatic geographic redundancy with minimal operational effort.
Column17: Core OCI Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: In Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), under the shared responsibility model, which of the following tasks is primarily the responsibility of Oracle, not the customer?
Column3: Configuring security lists and network firewalls
Column4: Customers are responsible for network configuration, including security lists and VCN firewalls. Exam trap: assuming Oracle provides all network security by default.
Column5: Installing patches and updates on compute instances
Column6: Customers are responsible for operating system and application patching. Oracle manages the underlying infrastructure only.
Column7: Encrypting sensitive data stored in OCI Object Storage
Column8: Customers can manage encryption keys using OCI Vault or BYOK, making encryption a customer responsibility.
Column9: Maintaining the physical security of OCI data centers
Column10: Oracle is responsible for physical access controls, surveillance, guards, and data center facilities as part of the shared responsibility model.
Column11: Managing user access permissions through IAM policies
Column12: Customers manage IAM policies, compartments, and access control for users and services.
Column16: Under the shared responsibility model, Oracle secures the physical infrastructure while customers secure configurations, data, and access.
Column17: Security Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: A fintech startup is migrating its payment processing application to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) and must comply with PCI DSS standards for handling credit card transactions. The company needs to ensure data encryption, enforce strict access control, and monitor all administrative and user activities for audit purposes. Which OCI service configuration best fulfills these requirements?
Column3: Object Storage with default encryption, Security Lists for network security, Internet Gateway for external access, and Local Peering Gateway for on-premises connection.
Column4: Default encryption may not meet PCI DSS key management requirements. Security Lists and gateways do not provide application-layer protection or detailed audit trails. Exam trap: assuming default encryption is sufficient.
Column5: Vault for managing encryption keys, Identity and Access Management (IAM) for role-based access control, Audit for logging user and administrator actions, and Web Application Firewall (WAF) for protecting sensitive data.
Column6: Vault ensures encryption key management, IAM enforces access control, Audit logs all activity, and WAF protects sensitive data in transit. Matches OCI best practices and PCI DSS requirements.
Column7: Block Storage without encryption, NAT Gateway for public access, Network Security Groups (NSGs) for traffic filtering, and IAM groups for limited access.
Column8: Unencrypted storage violates PCI DSS. Network controls alone do not meet encryption and audit requirements.
Column9: Object Storage without encryption, Security Lists for access control, DRG for connecting to on-premises resources, and Audit for logging system events.
Column10: Unencrypted storage and lack of key management make this non-compliant despite audit logging.
Column16: PCI DSS compliance in OCI requires Vault-managed encryption, IAM access control, Audit logging, and WAF protection.
Column17: Security Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: A financial services company is migrating sensitive customer records to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). To comply with industry regulations, they must ensure that all stored data and all communications between services are encrypted by default. Which OCI feature should the company leverage to centrally manage encryption keys and enforce encryption across its cloud resources?
Column4: Audit tracks API calls and user activity but does not encrypt data or manage encryption keys. Exam trap: confusing monitoring with enforcement.
Column6: Central service for creating, storing, and managing encryption keys. Enables encryption of data at rest and integrates with services for in-transit encryption, aligning with regulatory requirements.
Column7: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Web Application Firewall (WAF)
Column8: WAF protects web applications from attacks but does not manage encryption or keys.
Column10: Security Zones enforce policy compliance but do not manage encryption keys or automatically encrypt data.
Column16: When encryption of data at rest and in transit is required, OCI Key Management is the correct service to manage and enforce encryption keys.
Column17: Security Services, Data Protection, Governance and Administration

Column1: 34. In Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), which of the following services is not primarily used for processing, analyzing, or managing data? Note: There is 1 correct answer to this question.
Column4: Used to extract, transform, and load (ETL) data for analytics workflows. Exam trap: It integrates with analytics services, so it seems “infrastructure-like” but is indeed analytics-focused.
Column6: Purpose-built for large-scale data analytics using Hadoop/Spark clusters. Correctly categorized as a data analytics service.
Column8: Serverless compute service designed for running event-driven code. Does not directly perform analytics or process datasets for analytics purposes. Reference: OCI Functions Documentation.
Column10: Helps organize, classify, and manage metadata for data analytics. Provides visibility and governance for analytics-ready data.
Column12: Used to store data that can be consumed by analytics services. While primarily storage, it supports analytics workflows (not the trick answer).
Column16: Focus on service purpose: analytics services handle, transform, or process data, while compute or network services do not directly perform analytics.
Column17: Getting Started with OCI, Core OCI Services, Security Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: 35. A global e-commerce platform plans to deploy a recommendation engine and user profile service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The system requires massive scalability for high-volume read/write operations, low-latency access across multiple regions, automatic scaling during traffic spikes, and flexible schema support to store diverse user behavior data. Which OCI Database service is the most appropriate choice? Note: There is 1 correct answer to this question.
Column4: Optimized for OLTP transactional workloads. Supports moderate scaling but not ideal for massive high-throughput, globally distributed key-value workloads. Exam trap: Candidates often confuse ATP with NoSQL because both support high performance transactions.
Column6: Suitable for relational workloads with structured data. Limited horizontal scaling for global high-throughput scenarios. Does not natively provide global low-latency replication.
Column8: Designed for high-volume read/write operations. Supports global replication for low-latency access. Automatic scaling for unpredictable workloads. Flexible schema allows storing diverse user behavior data efficiently. Reference: OCI NoSQL Database Overview.
Column10: Optimized for analytical workloads, not high-velocity transactional reads/writes. Best for complex queries on large datasets but not low-latency global operations.
Column16: High read/write throughput plus global access plus flexible schema equals OCI NoSQL Database.
Column17: Core OCI Services, Database Services, Getting Started with OCI

Column1: 36. You are designing a highly available web application in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). You want to ensure that your compute instances and storage are isolated from infrastructure failures. Which statement correctly describes an Availability Domain? Note: There is 1 correct answer to this question.
Column3: A network segment within a Virtual Cloud Network (VCN) that distributes traffic between compute instances.
Column4: This describes a subnet, not an Availability Domain. Exam trap: confusing VCN/subnet boundaries with AD boundaries.
Column5: A single, isolated data center within an OCI Region that operates independently with its own power and network.
Column6: Correct definition of an Availability Domain. Reference: OCI Documentation – Availability Domains.
Column7: A global Oracle Cloud location that contains multiple Regions for disaster recovery.
Column8: This describes Oracle Cloud Regions or Region pairs, not ADs. Misconception: Candidates often think AD equals region-level DR solution.
Column9: A logical grouping of multiple compute instances across Regions for load balancing.
Column10: This is a logical compute deployment or global load balancing, unrelated to AD definition.
Column16: AD equals a single isolated data center in a region with independent power and network.
Column17: Getting Started with OCI, Core OCI Services, Security Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: 37. A global research organization wants to expand its operations on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Their priorities include enforcing security and compliance standards automatically across multiple compartments, receiving alerts for non-compliant resources, and reducing cloud security management overhead for a small IT team. Which OCI service is the most appropriate choice for this scenario? Note: There is 1 correct answer to this question.
Column4: Security Zones enforce strict rules at the compartment level for resource deployment. They are more rigid and do not provide automated monitoring or remediation across existing resources. Exam trap: confusing Security Zones enforcement with Cloud Guard automated monitoring.
Column6: Continuously monitors OCI resources for misconfigurations and security risks. Automatically enforces security and compliance policies across regions and compartments. Reduces manual governance effort. Reference: OCI Cloud Guard Overview.
Column8: Collects logs and events but does not automatically enforce policies or compliance. Useful for auditing and diagnostics, not governance automation.
Column10: Automates infrastructure deployment via Terraform, not compliance enforcement. Exam trap: Candidates might think it helps enforce standards, but it is deployment-focused.
Column12: Provides visibility into costs and usage trends but does not enforce security or compliance policies.
Column16: OCI Cloud Guard provides automated governance, compliance monitoring, and remediation.
Column17: Governance and Administration, Security Services, Core OCI Services

Column1: 38. Which two Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) services provide fully managed database solutions that automatically handle scaling, patching, and performance optimization? Select two.
Column4: Provides storage for objects, not a managed database. Object Storage does not manage database workloads.
Column6: Fully managed, self-tuning transactional database. Handles patching, scaling, backups, and performance automatically. Reference: OCI Autonomous Database Documentation.
Column8: Serverless compute service, not designed for database management.
Column10: Managed MySQL database with automated backups, high availability, and scaling. Reference: OCI MySQL Database Service.
Column12: Analytics and BI service, does not provide database management.
Column14: VMware workloads in OCI, unrelated to database operations.
Column16: Autonomous Database and MySQL Database Service are OCI managed databases with automatic scaling, patching, and optimization.
Column17: Getting Started with OCI, Core OCI Services, Security Services, Governance and Administration

Column1: 39. Which two OCI services help you monitor resources for potential security risks and enforce access controls in your cloud environment? Select two.
Column4: Manages encryption keys, but it does not actively monitor or enforce security policies. Exam trap: sounds security-related but is a supporting feature.
Column6: Detects misconfigurations and security risks across OCI resources and provides remediation. Reference: OCI Cloud Guard Documentation.
Column8: Controls data retention and archiving, not security monitoring.
Column10: Manages users, groups, roles, and policies. Central to access control and security governance. Reference: OCI IAM Documentation.
Column12: Scales compute resources based on load, not related to security.
Column14: Data processing service with no security posture management.
Column16: OCI Cloud Guard monitors security risks and IAM enforces access control.
Column17: Security Services, Governance, and Administration
